title: 2026 Made Bike Show Favs 01: Baphomet, English, Fiddlehead, Frances, Onguza, Rare Earth, Sycip, Woodpecker, Wilde Bikes – John Watson, Paul Kalifatidi, & Spencer Harding
content:
Team Radavist is on the ground at the 2026 Made Bike Show, documenting a selection of bikes. During load-in day, Spencer, Paul, and John perused the available offerings and selected bikes from Baphomet, English, Fiddlehead, Frances, Onguza, Rare Earth, Sycip, Woodpecker, and Wilde Bikes. Read on for a jam-packed gallery full of details of our favs from Day 01!

The Radavist thanks Shimano for sponsoring our Made Bike Show coverage and our independent Reportage!

Baphomet Bicycles Rainbow Abomination Hardtail – Paul Kalifatidi

Bellingham based builder, Dillen Wilder, came to Made with his Baphomet Bicycles Rainbow Abomination. This bike is being raffled off as a fundraiser for All Bikes Welcome, a non-profit that works to expand equity and belonging in cycling and the outdoors. You can support the good fight and join the raffle here. The bike is a “spicy medium” size and will fit riders who feel that such a description fits them.

Dillen wants the world to know that he isn’t really in the business of making bicycles, he is more in the business of giving them away for good causes. He also wants to help spread this disease that afflicts him. If you’re ever looking for help in learning how to start making bikes, Dillen has one open heart and two open ears.

Dillen worked with SRAM, Rockshox, Wolf Tooth Components, Paul Components, Velocity Wheels, Teravail, Doom Bars, and Loam Equipment to build the bike. A smorgasbord of meticulously mismatched rainbow componentry contrast against the black oxide raw steel frame.

Dillen doesn’t file his brazes (unless you ask really nicely) which can be somewhat contrarian. Yet, I think it is decisions like this that make his bikes stand out. In a venue filled with the most elegant and beautiful craftsmanship that this industry can display, Dillen’s approachable aesthetic feels like a palate cleanser.

And yes, there is no need to worry, he didn’t forget the pentagram.

@Baphomet_Bicycles

English Cycles Rob’s Personal 32″ – Spencer Harding

Rob is an absolute steel wizard, and I just really needed to shoot one of his truss fork bikes at the show; this one happened to be his personal 32” wheeled bike. It was designed for an especially long ride, and thus Rob endeavoured to get two bottles and a custom framebag into the triangle and two further bottles on the fork trusses. His goal was to carry nothing on his person for the ride.

The front end is a cluster of curved tubes, which finds the stem resting elegantly on the swooping trusses of the fork. Speaking of elegant, look at that seat tube bend. Where others bend or kink, Rob creates a swooping tube that allows for the incredible 440mm chainstays. Which, I may add, he accomplished without a yoke and with a 52mm chainline. Wizardry…

The cockpit sports gripshifts on both sides, with the left shifter being repurposed as a dropper post lever. The bike is dripping in orange anodization from Garbaruk, Madrone, Wolf Tooth, and Onyx. As Rob put it, “Every mountain bike needs an Onyx hub.” ‘Nuff said.

@Englishcycles

 

Fiddlehead Cycles Mini Velo Cargo Bike – John Watson

Portland, Oregon-based Fiddlehead Cycles began with its owner, Justin Foote, watching a few YouTube videos to learn the craft of frame building. After countless hours of practice, the engineer and fabricator finally began making custom bikes in 2023. Justin’s love for taking on truly custom builds.

Displayed at the Fiddlehead booth was this mini velo cargo bike, built for a customer in San Francisco. The customer wanted something capable yet compact and light-ish in weight. Lifting it off the stand and rolling it outdoors, the 46-pound total weight felt surprising compared to other cargo bikes I’ve documented and owned throughout the years.

For components, the client wanted a Pinion Smart.Shift system, carbon Velo Duo fenders, 650b rear, 20″ front wheel, and a Bike Technology suspension fork. The webbing for the platform – that also pivots to take up less space in the client’s apartment – was made by Lords Luggage.

@FiddleheadCycles

Frances Cycles Trishaw and Farfarer -Spencer Harding

Joshua Muir holds a special place in my history with bikes. I distinctly remember ogling his cable-steered cargo bikes over a decade ago in front of the Bike Church in Santa Cruz. His ingenuity was undeniable in my eyes then, and that has stayed true to this day. His Trishaw and accompanying Farfarer trailer was like a tractor-trailer in bike form.

Josh encouraged me to take the bike for a spin, and I was instantly smitten as it was one of the oddest bikes I’ve ever ridden. The headtube lies at a negative angle, which he described as a Malaysian design, which causes the fork, er basket, er front end (?) to find its way back to straight naturally. It was more akin to a swing bike than anything else I could possibly describe. It brought a smile to my face. Josh made sure to note that the wood was all reclaimed from his local dump. Reclaimed or not, the wood added such a warm touch to shooting typically metallic bikes.

With is ability to swing and “fold” over the front of the bike, easy track offroad, and carry an impressive load, the Farfarer trailers remain the pinnacle of a bicycle trailer design.

@FrancesCycles

 

Onguza 32″ Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Onguza hails from Namibia, and much like the charismatic mega fauna that roam that land, this big wheeled bike is perfectly suited to the rough and rolling terrain of the African savanna. Onguza was started by Dan Craven and is owned by him and Onguza’s master framebuilders, Petrus Mufenge and Sakaria Nkolo. Onguza stole the show for me back in 2023, and I desperately wish to see another herd of Onguza bicycles some day. For now, we’ll have to enjoy the occasional sighting in the dark depths of Zidell Yards.

Onguza worked with Billy Sinkford, the director and co-founder of Made, to refine their 32″ gravel bike design. While 32″ wheels might not be for everyone, they are certainly everywhere at this year’s show. Namibia is filled with rough dirt roads and the rolling terrain that seems to best suit the adaptation of giant hoops, so seeing this bike at the show as a no-brainer. It is also one of the of the official Made show bikes.

This bike is built up with the increasingly tasteful and increasingly rare combination of Paul Clamper disc brakes to SRAM Force AXS shifters. An XX Transmission Drivetrain is turned by a White Industries crankset. Paul Components, Camp And Go Slow, and Silca round out the build. While many of the Onguzas that I have witnessed have had bright and patterned finishes, this is the most muted one that I have seen. It’s understated and I love it.

@OnguzaBicycles

Rare Earth 32″ Crazy Cloud Full Suspension – Paul Kalifatidi

As a fellow Wisconsinite, I feel a big-bite-from-a-fresh-slice-of-Ian’s-mac-and-cheese-pizza-with-the-cheese-stretching-from-mouth-to-slice-like connection through the dairy-filled fabric of space and time to Brian Hall, the builder of Rare Earth Cycle. Brian, I have no idea if you feel this too, sorry.

This year, there are a few Rare Earth bikes roaming the halls of Made. He has two of his own bikes at the show and he’s fully invested into the 32″ wheel for his own riding. This full suspension, the “Crazy Cloud,” is the one he rode at the Doom ultra-endurance race where finishers get a bell. It features 120mm of front suspension supplied by an Intend Samurai 32″ fork and a linkage driven single pivot that makes 110mm of rear suspension. A Madrone Jab derailleur handles the shifting and Berd Hawk30 Gold wheels do the spinning. Color matched Cyber Cycles cranks tie the build together.

Brian’s bikes rarely appear from this Earth. Tubes, thin and thick, meet at unfamiliar angles. Yet, somehow, after stepping away from the craft, there is the instantly recognizable silhouette of a Rare Earth. I am constantly in awe of how he uses various materials and textures to achieve his vision in a way that is always consistent with his design language. Brian, well done. Your work is as timeless as 25-year cheddar.

@RareEarth_Cycle

Sycip Designs PR32DATOR – Spencer Harding

Jeremy came this year with a fresh bike from a repeat customer, whose Strava name is Apex Predator, hence the word/number play Pr32ator. The finish is an ecstatic green sparkle with glow-in-the-dark decals, which I couldn’t manage to find a way to photograph. The chainstays feature steel pennies from WWII, which the customer provided instead of the usual copper pennies Jeremy utilizes.

In a playful mix of new and old, the bike features a 1 ⅛” straight headtube paired with 32” wheels. The Pr32ator has an intriguing mix of internal routing in the main triangle and external routing on the rear triangle and fork. Me oh my look at all of these barrel adjusters, I must be in heaven. This is one of the most unique cable routing ideas I’ve ever seen.

With the specificity and oddball details of this bike, it’s hard to overlook what I can assume is a trusting relationship between the builder and customer. Jeremy delivered an amazing bike with tons of eccentric detailing in a package I can only imagine rides as well as it sparkles.

@SycipDesgins

 

Woodpecker Cycle Co Mini Velo – John Watson

Darren from Woodpecker Cycle Co has been teasing this mini velo for months, sending me sneak peeks on Instagram. “I hope more people bring kook bikes to this show,” he exclaimed while documenting the bike. Cold agree right here. In fact, I want most of the bikes I document at the 2026 Made Bike Show to be exactly that: kook bikes. Darren’s attitude and vibe are exactly what has drawn me to documenting framebuilders: creative, unapologetic, fun, and kooky.

This bike features a Pinion gearbox, with a custom 3D-printed shifter, inspired by the old Schwinn Stik Shift. Darren explained how he actually broke the hardware attempting to make the shifter during his first attempt. If it weren’t for the US importer of Pinion, who gave him the last older-style shifter in the US, this detail might not have happened. Pinion’s newer design has the cables coming out in the other direction, but these older shifters allow for the clean cable routing as shown. He also designed the bike’s headbadge.

“Can you wheelie it?” I asked, and Darren replied, “Nah, it’s a customer’s bike; I don’t wanna thrash it.” Fair enough! This bike’s owner, Jeremy, works for Teravail, which supplied some yet-to-be-released products for the build, along with Onyx, which debuted its new knurled headset and supplied hubs. “Those disc rotors would be great for camping if you wanted to strain spaghetti,” he joked, noting the Japanese market Hope discs. Corey Thomson of Thompson Cycles helped with the fork and the build is 10/10 no notes.

For Darren’s first mini velo, I say he knocked it out of the park. All hail the kook bike. Stunning job, Darren!

@WoodpeckerCycleCo

Wilde Bikes Pleezer Breezer Series I Homage – John Watson

Obtaining a Breezer Series I would be nearly impossible. Joe Breeze only built ten from 1977 and 1978. When Wilde Bikes investor Andy Tesch saw Scot Nicol’s Breezer when visiting Ibis Cycles last year, he expressed a desire to own one, but he knew they were unobtainium. Instead of making a direct 26″ wheel copy, he opted for a boost-spaced 29er. The modern SRAM 1987 Eagle Transmission looks so damn good, too!

While talking with Brad Wilson, Wilde’s US operation’s builder, he expressed that he took some creative liberties, deviating from Joe Breeze’s original design. He kept the 1″ headset spec, but I immediately knew what he was referring to. In a classic Breezer Series I, the lateral tubes are attached to the seat tube. Brad opted to let these tubes “float,” hoping the thin-walled tubing would flex and float a bit more. Attaching the tubes would stiffen it up more.

Brad also made the Wilde bullmoose quill stem and used Paragon dropouts on the front and rear of the bike. I must say, I’ve seen a number of Breezer homages, but this one is really special. A proper homage, in my opinion, takes the vibe of the original’s form and modernizes the function. The proportions of a Breezer Series I as a 29er look really damn good, and the nickel plating on the frameset is just the icing on the cake.

If you’d like to pre-order a “Pleezer,” Wilde Bikes has them on its website for a cooooool $5,800.

@WildeBikes

 

 

Well, that’s a wrap for our first 2026 Made Bike Show gallery. Which bike is your favorite, and what would you like to see us document from the show?
